answer.rationale:
The competitor's entry pricing makes promotional_pricing the emotionally obvious response, and memory_73 is the most quantitatively seductive record in the inheritance (+31% new accts, +18% booked rev, 12 cohorts). That is exactly why it is the first verification pull: every metric it reports is an acquisition-side metric measured at the moment of purchase. It says nothing about retention, expansion, or revenue quality 2-3 quarters out, and it explicitly notes the buyers acquired were price-sensitive. Discounting to win price-sensitive buyers away from a cheaper competitor is the classic way to book short-term revenue that decays into churn — a direct conflict with the stated objective of *sustainable long-term qualified* revenue. I want the original record to see whether retention was ever measured or merely unobserved; 'no measurable harm' language appears in memory_57, not memory_73, which is itself telling.

Second pull is memory_86, because it underwrites my intended action and I should verify what I lean on, not only what I reject. Onboarding completion (-4%) plausibly sits upstream of the activation drop (-6%): accounts that never finish onboarding cannot activate. Fixing the upstream constraint may recover both, whereas activation_messaging (memory_91) treats the downstream symptom in a population that onboarding is already leaking. But memory_86's headline metrics — completion rate, time-to-value — are proxies, not qualified revenue. Shortening onboarding can raise completion by removing the very qualification and configuration steps that make an account durable, converting a genuine improvement into a metric that looks better while the cohort is worse. I want the source record to check whether downstream retention or revenue was tracked, or whether completion was the terminal measurement.

Setting aside the other candidates: referral_incentive (memory_57) targets established customers and does not address either declining metric; enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is a different segment entirely from the SMB accounts under competitive attack. Both are plausible but off-problem this week.

Standing uncertainties I am not resolving: these memories are consolidated summaries whose original context and confounds are largely stripped, they span days 12-61 under different market conditions than day 76, and none of them was measured against long-term qualified revenue. Two of the six (memory_31, memory_86) make overlapping onboarding claims that may derive from one underlying result rather than two independent confirmations. I therefore run this as a standard experiment with retention and revenue-quality holdouts carried past the completion metric, not as a broad rollout — and if memory_86 turns out to have terminated at completion rate, I will drop to a guarded test rather than treat the inherited lift as established. If memory_73 unexpectedly contains real long-horizon retention data, promotional_pricing becomes defensible and I would revisit.
